papers.title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

papers.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
papers.abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

papers.title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark
papers.abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

papers.title: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
papers.abstract: Personalized generative retrieval in search should jointly satisfy the user's immediate search intent and long-term preference. Recent end-to-end approaches, primarily explored in recommendation, unify item tokenization and sequence generation within a single model, allowing semantic identifiers (SIDs) to be optimized toward the downstream generation objective. However, these methods often treat the query merely as an input feature, without explicitly leveraging it to guide either identifier learning or sequence generation. This leaves intent guidance weak in both the tokenization and the generation stage, causing generated semantic identifiers to drift toward high-frequency token patterns rather than the current search intent. In this work, we find that incorporating additional query-related evidence into the framework of end-to-end generative retrieval is important. Based on this finding, we propose IntentGR, an intent-enhanced end-to-end framework that strengthens query semantics at four complementary stages of the retrieval pipeline. Query-Aware Semantic Behavior Representation (QBR) introduces query-level behavioral evidence as a new input signal; Query-Semantic Alignment (QSA), Long-Tail Query Enrichment (LQE), and Query-conditioned Attention Modulation (QAM) then serve as integration mechanisms at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages to fully exploit this evidence. Experiments on the public AOL4PS benchmark and AE, a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, show that IntentGR improves Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with strong gains on long-tail queries. These results suggest that enriched query-related input evidence, together with effective integration mechanisms, is beneficial for building intent-aware end-to-end generative search systems.

papers.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
papers.abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

papers.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
papers.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

papers.title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
papers.abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
papers.abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

papers.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
papers.abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

papers.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
papers.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

papers.title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.

papers.title: Attribution Through the Decoder: Prediction-Space Explanations for Structured Outputs
papers.abstract: Networks that predict angles, gaze directions, and rotations do not output these quantities directly: they emit raw coordinates that a fixed decoder, such as normalization, maps to the final prediction. Attribution methods are usually applied to the raw coordinates, so they can credit inputs for changes the decoder discards, such as rescaling a vector when only its direction matters. The resulting explanation can highlight inputs that have no effect on the prediction. We instead attribute through the decoder differential, which for normalization decoders reduces to a scaled tangent projection. We characterize invariance to output rescaling, show that every fixed smooth scalar target on a sphere has points of zero tangential sensitivity, and show that an endpoint-projected variant of Integrated Gradients can still attribute to scale-only inputs, whereas direct angular Integrated Gradients cannot. On synthetic tasks with analytically known relevance, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to an irrelevant region. On MPIIGaze validation data, tangent Grad-CAM produces 44% greater prediction displacement under 10% pixel deletion. On PASCAL3D+ with a 6D rotation decoder, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over the ambient coordinate sum and by 13.8 degrees over a decoder-invariant scalar. Results for a two-polarity tangent LayerCAM variant are mixed: it exceeds ambient-sum LayerCAM on circular regression but no difference is detected on quaternion pose. These results separate two failure sources, radial contamination and scalarization loss. The approach uses existing attribution methods with decoder-aware targets, although some variants also require changes to attribution aggregation. An invariant attribution can still miss inputs that drive the prediction, so invariance and deletion performance should each be checked.

papers.title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
papers.abstract: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

papers.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. papers.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

papers.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
papers.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

papers.title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.

papers.title: A Full-Ledger Counterfactual Audit of Adaptive Reasoning
papers.abstract: Adaptive reasoning must decide whether to answer now or spend more compute. Predicting that the current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will improve it. We introduce the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA), which compares an immediate answer with four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under one answer procedure and accounts for the cost of every signal used by a policy. On GSM8K and MATH-500, a random 256-token continuation recovers a wrong answer in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B cases, while damaging a correct answer in 1.4% and 1.9%. Correctness labels from independently sampled continuations predict a separate continuation's outcome in both primary models. In offline replay, using these labels to allocate compute improves performance on DeepSeek; the Qwen3 gain remains inconclusive. Under full cost accounting, the tested lightweight, myopic controllers mainly recognize current errors and add little continuation-specific value beyond that shortcut. A Llama-8B replication and action/cost ablations examine the robustness of these findings. FLCVA separates measuring local continuation value, predicting it from observable signals, and using those predictions to allocate computation.

papers.title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
papers.abstract: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage. We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

papers.title: From Relevance to Utility: Rubric Alignment in Yuanbao Search
papers.abstract: Agentic search demands that a search engine move beyond per document relevance ranking to assemble document sets optimized for downstream LLM reasoning. Prior work addresses this either by improving individual pipeline stages in isolation or by applying RL based selection on top of relevance trained upstream modules, leaving the full stack unaligned to utility for reasoning. We propose rubric aligned search, a framework that unifies the traditional search pipeline under a single supervision surface. For each query, we derive a rubric from coarse to fine, specifying weighted positive criteria that the document set must satisfy and negative criteria that it must avoid. From this rubric we derive two training signals. First, a lightweight labeler distills rubric grounded judgments into per document utility labels, which supervise a contrastive dual encoder for retrieval and a multi task ranker trained with four rubric aligned scoring heads. Second, a rubric conditioned evaluator produces a set level reward that drives a dual branch RL selector, combining GRPO with best rollout distillation to resolve credit assignment in subset optimization. Deployed in Yuanbao Search, the pipeline improves end to end answer quality by 8.52% over the online production baseline.

papers.title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
papers.abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.

papers.title: MIPR: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Multimodal Intent-to-Product Retrieval with Multi-Category Solutions
papers.abstract: Real-world e-commerce queries often express user intent without naming a target product, and a single intent may be fulfilled by products from multiple categories. However, existing multimodal retrieval benchmarks typically assume a relatively well-defined target, leaving retrieval for intents with multi-category solutions less explored. To fill this gap, we introduce MIPR, a benchmark for Multimodal Intent-to-Product Retrieval comprising 3,522 multimodal queries and a shared corpus of 30,731 products. MIPR features reasoning-intensive retrieval, multi-category solutions, and fine-grained relevance labels. Experiments show that the best embedding-based retriever achieves 49.23% nDCG@10 on the full query set, and 55.86% solution-category recall@10 on queries with multiple solution categories. Reranking improves these scores to 60.11% and 67.00%, respectively, yet substantial gaps to the candidate-pool oracle remain. These results establish MIPR as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for evaluating multimodal intent-to-product retrieval. The data and code are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/leequeue/MIPR.

papers.title: Learning Cross-Domain Media Similarity from Amazon Reviews
papers.abstract: Collaborative filtering is a basic foundation of many recommendation algorithms. It works by analyzing a user's history and then suggesting items similar to those in that history. This method typically relies on user data to compute item similarity, data that is widely available to commercial systems but is usually sparse or inaccessible for independent systems and research, especially across multiple media domains. In this work, we propose a method to generalize similarity information between items using supervised learning. As input to our model, we use semantic and temporal features extracted from Amazon product reviews, which are publicly available. As the training target, we use item (product) co-occurrence in the reviewing history of Amazon customers. We evaluate the quality of the predicted similarities across two media domains: books and movies. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness of our methodology, yielding positive outcomes in zero-shot cross-domain transfer tasks. Furthermore, feature attribution analysis reveals a structural shift in how feature groups are utilized across setups: intra-domain models rely heavily on linguistic semantics, whereas cross-domain environments pivot toward behavioral popularity cues. Incorporating even limited target-domain context during training bridges this domain sparsity gap, significantly enhancing framework generalization.

papers.title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

papers.title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP), and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: nearest-neighbor status can be separated from passage-like meaning. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by how reliably their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence.

papers.title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
papers.abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences, and Applications (ACDSA 2027)

papers.title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
papers.abstract: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.

papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

papers.title: SIMQ: A Single Graph-based Index for Multi-Vector Query
papers.abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness by representing documents as sets of token-level vectors and scoring via MaxSim, but their high computational cost limits scalability to large corpora. Existing approximate methods face fundamental bottlenecks: centroid interaction matrix approaches require computing a full matrix at every query and rely on GPU-accelerated clustering, while data-oblivious compression methods yield unstable recall that requires repeated compensation. We propose SIMQ (Single graph Index for Multi-vector Query), a framework that bridges single-vector graph indices and multi-vector retrieval through data-aware sampling-based clustering and per-token graph navigation, simultaneously bypassing all aforementioned bottlenecks. SIMQ organizes all token vectors into fine-grained clusters via data-aware sampling, builds a single graph index over cluster centroids independently of PLAID's residual representation, and approximates the MaxSim score through per-token graph search without materializing any interaction matrix or relying on GPU acceleration. We provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a manifold assumption and successful cell retrieval, data-aware partitioning has a smaller expected approximation error than a data-oblivious partition. Building on this foundation, SIMQ+ further introduces count-based scoring and a dynamic candidate set to improve robustness across varying query conditions. Experiments on five benchmarks compare recall, throughput, and construction time against several baselines, primarily on CPU; large-scale PLAID k-means centroids are built on a separate GPU machine. SIMQ has been integrated into VSAG, an Ant Group's open-source vector search library.

papers.title: Cluster-Guided Decoding with Trust-Region Constraints for Personalized Recommendation
papers.abstract: Most recommenders score each item in the catalog separately, and do not explicitly model which semantic region of the catalog a recommendation belongs to. Models expressive enough to offer that control are often too slow to run over a full catalog for online inference. In this paper, we present Cluster-Guided Generative Reconstruction (CG2R), which learns a hierarchy of semantic clusters and uses a cluster-level prior to steer item ranking for personalized recommendations. Unlike existing systems that only use clusters to pre-select candidates, CG2R adds the cluster prior directly to the item scoring rule, so that the learned cluster structure shapes the ranking itself. Because the prior is assembled from cluster centroids rather than per-item statistics, it remains defined even for cold-start users when no history is available. Across the three benchmark datasets evaluated, CG2R outperforms classical, neural, and LLM-based baselines in terms of Recall and nDCG, with its performance gains widening as the catalog grows sparser. In addition, CG2R serves recommendations in milliseconds, suggesting potential as low-latency first-stage retrieval.

papers.title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

papers.title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
papers.abstract: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

papers.title: More Than a Score: Reinforcement Learning with Verbalized Feedback for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users' interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.

papers.title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommenders decode the semantic ID of a user's next item with a language model, and post-training them with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice. The gains are mostly reported on the first ten results, yet in deployment such models hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker or reward model. We show that RL post-training has a hidden cost: it improves accuracy at the top of the list (hit@K for small K) but, on all five datasets we study, lowers the recall of the candidate list (hit@K for K in the hundreds). The model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. Controlled experiments trace the loss to the negative advantages that RL assigns to the candidates it samples, the rollout. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.

papers.title: Music Similarity Learning in Sparse Latin Scenarios
papers.abstract: In this work we propose a lightweight, interpretable approach that estimates item-item music similarity from publicly available metadata. Our hybrid regression model combines content-based filtering with the classic item-based collaborative filtering. We test generalization via a zero-shot evaluation on Latin American music, a genre for which co-occurrence data is scarce. Accurately predicting similarity for these unseen, sparse pairs shows that our approach is robust to the regional gap affecting many existing systems, without the audio signal processing or the computational budget that deep multimodal approaches would require.

papers.title: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification
papers.abstract: A rare label seldom occurs alone, and a classifier can recover it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without having learned the label itself. Existing diagnostics of this need a trained model: none says before training whether a corpus admits the failure, or what the standard aggregate hides. Macro-F1, like any measure built from per-label confusion counts, is unchanged by how a label's recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion. We introduce a within-label estimand of that division, a reading rule under which a fall in dependence counts only if companion-free recall rises, and a statistic of training labels that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined. Up to 18.4% of the tail true positives macro-F1 credits would vanish at the companion-free rate, within the training-label bound on every corpus. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture moves it. Models whose tail score is computed from other labels' predictions are strongly dependent.
papers.comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Submitted to Information Sciences

papers.title: CARE: Conversational Affective Response Retrieval for Internet Memes
papers.abstract: Conversational meme retrieval supports response selection in online communication, where relevance depends on both contextual meaning and affective expression. We study this task using two language-specific collections from Douban and Imgflip, containing 98,506 meme records across 5,583 discussion topics. Thread membership supplies weak relevance labels, while likes provide implicit ranking feedback. Automatically extracted sentiment, facial-expression indicators, and cross-modal consistency features support an exploratory analysis of engagement. We propose CARE, a Conversational Affective Response Retrieval framework that combines an emotion-enhanced CLIP retriever with a Jina-based reranker. The retriever incorporates free-form emotion descriptors through gated fusion and learns from multiple positive examples per query. The reranker combines query--image interactions with emotion representations and is trained using engagement-based ranking supervision. Under the reported topic-held-out protocol, CARE achieves Hit@10 of 24.03\% on Douban and 49.33\% on Imgflip, compared with 23.16\% and 41.07\%, respectively, for fine-tuned CLIP. These results support the utility of the complete two-stage system for recovering thread-associated memes. They do not independently establish perceived social resonance or isolate the contribution of affect from reranker training. The study provides a basis for further evaluation of affect-aware retrieval with human relevance judgments and controlled comparisons.

papers.title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning
papers.abstract: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.

papers.title: User First Intelligence: Three Measurements of Search and AI-Answer Analytics (SEO and GEO/AEO), and a Knowledge-Graph Framework for Query Discovery Beyond Search Volume
papers.abstract: People say what they want to know in many places besides a search box, and the tools that search and AI-answer optimization (SEO and GEO/AEO) rely on see only part of that demand, through models reported as counts. This paper reports three measurements of such instruments and a framework. On the area-code section of a large US telecom provider's site, two commercial analytics platforms differed on estimated monthly visits by 7.5x to 27.1x (8.6x to 29.9x worldwide); across twelve sections of the domain the ratio ran from 0.20x to 7.24x with no detectable relation to section age, while they agreed on which section is larger in 60 of 66 pairs. On 37,193 reviews of 378 telecom stores linked to a 42,994-node keyword taxonomy, review demand and search volume agreed on branches to a varying degree (Spearman 0.47 to 0.75; 0.91 post hoc) and barely on topics (0.18), on links two blind AI annotators judged two-thirds correct; on the 372 area codes, a public count of Wikipedia requests for each code and vendor volume agreed roughly on ranking (0.45 over 240 articles, gone once keywords matched per code are held constant) and not on magnitudes, predictions fixed first. In one vendor's index of AI answers naming or citing the largest companies of each S&P 500 sector, of four predictions written first, one held, one in direction only and two failed; video and community sites took a median 21% of citation incidences on Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode against 0.6% to 9.2% on four other surfaces, in every sector, and in education answers in each of 13 countries read later. Estimates and sources need measuring per instrument and surface. User First Intelligence (UFI), built on that premise, collects what people ask beyond the website, links it to an industry ontology and scores where an organization does not answer; an open implementation is released, its score not evaluated. No causal claim is made.
papers.comment: 43 pages, 10 figures. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Data and scripts in the ancillary files; implementation at https://github.com/VenkataPagadalaGIT/ufi

papers.title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
papers.abstract: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.
papers.comment: Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale: Data Attribution and Provenance (ATTRIB 2026) at NeurIPS 2026, Idea Track. 4 pages main text, 13 pages total, 1 figure, 2 tables

papers.title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
papers.abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.
papers.comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Accepted to appear in Proc. of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026), Phoenix, AZ, USA. This is the author's accepted manuscript

papers.title: Explainable Federated Learning via Global-Local Attribution Alignment
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables on-device training without centralizing data, yet existing systems still struggle to provide explanations that are both locally faithful and globally consistent under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints. Prior approaches either keep explanations siloed across clients, transmit heavy or sensitive artifacts, or replace expressive task models with interpretable surrogates that sacrifice accuracy. We propose xFedAlign, a model-agnostic framework that decouples task optimization in parameter space from explanation coordination in a compact group space. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate to produce private, per-class top-k attribution artifacts, which are robustly aggregated by the server into a Global Explanation Prior that softly aligns client explanations without constraining task learning. Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with IID and non-IID partitions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while consistently reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC relative to Local-XAI, FedAttr-Agg, and Fed-XAI, with only a few kilobytes of additional communication per round. Privacy and robustness evaluations further demonstrate reduced membership inference advantage and increased resistance to attribution poisoning, enabling consistent and trustworthy explanations in federated learning.
papers.comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Published in Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.
papers.comment: 9 pages. Accepted as an oral presentation at the AI4F workshop, ICAIF 2026, Milan

papers.title: DetouR: Plugging Association Routes into Search Agents for Multi-hop Question Answering
papers.abstract: Search agents answer multi-hop questions by interleaving reasoning with retrieval, deciding at each step what to search next. Existing agents follow semantic routes: they infer what is missing and phrase it as a query, reaching only what the model can name. Yet the decisive page is often one the question never names, frequently just one hyperlink away from evidence already retrieved. Following such association routes reaches more gold pages than semantic search under the same budget. Exploiting them raises two challenges: obtaining the association structure without costly offline graph construction, and keeping linked evidence in the reader's limited context, where relevance- and fusion-based selection discards it. We propose DetouR, a plug-in that reuses the links arriving with retrieved pages and adds no search or LLM call. Link Rerouting replaces near-repeat queries with routes to linked pages, chosen by a lightweight learned scorer; Chain-aware Context Selection runs personalized PageRank over these links so that evidence chains reach the reader intact. Across four agents, DetouR improves EM by 4.0 points on 2Wiki and 1.4 on HotpotQA on average. We also find that heavier LLM models struggle with this non-semantic evidence, adding little over these simple selectors or even falling behind. In summary, our work reveals association routes as a cheap complement to semantic routes that current search agents overlook: added as a plug-in, they improve every agent we test, in replay and in live runs, at no extra search or LLM cost.

papers.title: EchoSpec: Training Search Agents to Weigh Evidence Above Echoes
papers.abstract: Search agents trained with reinforcement learning decide what to retrieve, when to search again, and when to answer. In real corpora, one claim is copied and paraphrased across many pages while the primary source settling a question appears once. We show that reinforcement-learned search agents grant echoes the credence of independent sources and lose their ability to abstain. Across five base models from 3B to 32B and seven released RL agents on multi-hop Wikipedia questions with primary evidence intact, eight paraphrased false-claim echoes overturn 58-73% of previously correct answers, while exact-match RL drives deleted-evidence abstention below 15%. Conditioning on retrieval localizes the failure to evidence acquisition: once primary evidence enters context, agents overrule eight echoes as reliably as one, whereas echoes fill top ranks and halt search early, so larger budgets, forced search turns, or passive passage filtering alone fail to recover displaced evidence. We introduce EchoSpec, specifying reliability across five corpus transformations with known target answers and training in two stages. Verification warm-start teaches multi-hop bridge-entity recovery past echoes, after which group RL optimizes an evidence-gated $λ$-reward with an outcome-independent acquisition bonus and scale-preserving advantages retaining the optimal rule $λ/(1+λ)$. Across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B backbones on nine evaluation suites, EchoSpec cuts eight-echo deference by 30-44 points on Qwen2.5-7B down to 29-31%, nearly quadruples eight-echo reach to 26-27% with zero-shot transfer to unseen BGE and BM25 retrievers, and raises standalone QA precision to 47-55%. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/unihsy/EchoSpec.

papers.title: DOCKET: A Pluralistic Benchmark for Evaluating AI-Assisted Policy Feedback in U.S. Rulemaking
papers.abstract: As AI models advance and impact deliberative democracies, there is a growing need to assess their support of pluralistic viewpoints. Most pluralism benchmarks are insufficient for this: they are not grounded in diversity (i.e., stakeholders across different frames, skills and needs), quality (i.e., rigorous and technical debates), and impact (i.e., invested deliberators and real-world outcomes). To address this, we first (i) curate DOCKET, the most comprehensive dataset of the U.S. Federal Notice & Comment process to date. DOCKET consists of 42.3M public comments on 22,400 regulations across 44 government agencies between 2016 and 2026 and contains millions of policy debates; we link public comments to particular policy items proposed by regulators to track the public's attention and the responsiveness of regulators to public input. (ii) Next, we demonstrate the pluralistic utility of DOCKET - we show that public commenters have a wide breadth of perspectives with significant depth in policy expertise and that regulators are often responsive. (iii) Finally, we present DOCKETBench, the first systematic evaluation of LLMs' ability to represent human policy perspectives in federal rulemaking. Only 18-30% of LLM-generated feedback aligns with real human comments. LLMs critique proposals broadly but generally, lacking the specific grounding, citations, and lived-experience arguments that humans bring to bear; in addition, most models we test systematically agree with government perspectives (overlapping with up to 68% of their claims) and agree least with labor unions (as little as 26% of their claims), demonstrating a fundamental skew in perspectives that even tools like persona modeling do not solve. Taken together, we reveal fundamental gaps in how language models navigate real policy issues, and DOCKETBench serves as a testbed for closing those gaps in a crucial real-world domain.

papers.title: Towards Explainable Sleep Stage Classification using Single-Channel Electroencephalogram
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging has achieved strong bench- mark accuracy; however, clinical adoption remains limited due to a lack of interpretability. In this work, we fill the research gap by extending the SleepXAI sleep staging framework to systematically compare five different XAI methods. Further, attribution fidelity is evaluated using Spearman rank correlation with AASM-defined EEG frequency bands, serving as clinically grounded reference signals. In this paper, we focus on single- channel Electroencephalogram (EEG), which is more amenable to practical clinical deployment compared to full polysomnography setups. Experiments are conducted on the Sleep-EDF benchmark dataset and the DREAMT dataset. In DREAMT, we stratified subjects based on OSA into four Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) severity groups. We observed that the SleepXAI model achieves strong classification performance on both datasets. Among the evaluated methods, Integrated Gradients (IG) consistently achieves the highest mean attribution fidelity across all five sleep stages on Sleep-EDF and across all AHI groups on DREAMT, outperforming all other evaluated methods under the Spearman rank correlation metric. These findings highlight the importance of attribution method selection as a key factor for ensuring reliable and clinically interpretable automated sleep staging systems.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at AgIA4BioHealth Workshop, IEEE BIBM 2026, Dallas, Texas, December 1-4, 2026

papers.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io

papers.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
papers.abstract: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights.
